fields.title: The Hunger Games
fields.description: A deeply dystopian series by Suzanne Collins, covering the problems of authoritarian government, desensitization, division, propaganda, and much more.
fields.summary:
Written by Suzanne Collins, this series explores the tension between authoritarian government and its oppressed subjects. Set in a future world post-United States where the new government and its upper-class (those living in "The Capitol") require two teenagers from each of the 12 Districts to be sent to certain death each year for the Hunger Games.

The Games pit these children from the Districts against each other in a kill or be killed situation that is also broadcast to the entire country as further propaganda and punishment for the Districts' rebellious past.

These books, including the original trilogy and the two new additions: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes and Sunrise on the Reaping are excellent and pertinent explorations of our humanity, our biases, how we are influenced or indoctrinated by narratives, and how we can make choices under extreme duress.

fields.title: Apophany
fields.description: Perceiving patterns out of noise—even when the patterns don't actually exist or connect.
fields.summary:
Perceiving patterns out of noise—even when the patterns don't actually exist or connect. Basis of conspiracy theory thinking.

For example, if you are motivated to find a connection between disparate information, you likely can come up with a through-line. However, if the conclusions are unsubstantiated or made up, then you haven't found "the truth."

It reminds of me of the Rorschach inkblots, where people perceive objects or even concepts when looking at random, ambiguous patterns.

fields.title: Critical Thinking
fields.summary: The ability to think about a concept in multiple ways; through multiple viewpoints. To slowly arrive at a conclusion after gathering multi-sourced arguments and evidence. Ideally this leads to making updates and corrections to your thoughts and conclusions as more / better information is discovered.

fields.title: Agency
fields.summary: The ability to act of one's own will.

fields.title: Cognitive Offloading
fields.description: Storing information somewhere other than in your own memory.
fields.summary:
Our brains collect so much junk over time that it interferes with our focus, our productivity, and our default ruminations. Cognitive offloading will empty the garbage can in our minds and open up space for clarity, purpose, intention. This can be done as easily as writing something down.

It is important to note that delegating information storage to something else (like a note system or digital storage) runs the risk of being harder to remember when you can't access the thing that holds the information.
fields.sources: Offloading items from memory: individual differences in cognitive offloading in a short-term memory task

fields.title: Religion
fields.description: Broadly speaking, the spiritual and / or mystical aspects of humanity.
fields.summary:
There's a flaw in Western terminology—most of what we might call "religion" is heavily influenced by Protestant Christianity. Religion isn't the best word, but I often don't have a better one to collect many ideas into one concept, but here is a small list of what is often a part of "religion" at least in CYBORG_.

  • Afterlife: What happens when we die?
  • Final Judgment: Eternal rewards and / or punishments
  • Ritual practices: Routines, prayers, credibility enhancing displays (CREDs)
  • Doctrine: Statements of belief or standards of beliefs (to be "in" XYZ religion, you need to believe this way about ABC)
  • In-group characteristics: Other things that indicate belonging to a group, such as clothing / appearance, speech and vernacular, values and standards.
  • Sacred objects: Things that are interacted with in some way and seen as part of worship, ritual or identity.

fields.title: Parkinson's Law
fields.description: Work expands to fill the time given to finish it.
fields.summary:
Two parts to this concept:

  1. You will find a way for the work you have to take the amount of time you have.

  2. Bureaucracy and officials don't want competition or rivals, they want subordinates. They create work for other people. The larger the scope of the office grows is not relative to the amount of work done or work that needs to be done.

fields.title: Ship of Theseus
fields.description: A paradox of being: are objects (or even ourselves) a matter of configured parts? What if you replace parts—do you eventually have a new thing or a new self?
fields.summary:
Paradox: if you have some thing and replace all of its parts one by one, do you still have the same thing by the end?

Called, "Ship of Theseus," because Plutarch posited that the Athenians preserved the ship that Theseus used to return from Crete by replacing parts as they decayed.

The 17th century philosopher, Thomas Hobbes, played with this paradox further by asking if someone gathered all of the old parts that were replaced and rebuilt the ship with those parts in all the same places, would that then become the "original" ship? Or is it the ship the one that was preserved by repairs and replacements?

fields.title: Social safety
fields.description: Your brain's first priority is your safety. Social safety isn't just the absence of danger, it's adding a buffer that we can feel trust and feel rest.
fields.summary:
Basic, social connection, acceptance, inclusion, and protection. You're part of a collective, not alone, someone has your back.

Fundamental to the human brain—we can't live alone. Our brains are wired for connection because we're social creatures.

fields.title: Prototype Theory
fields.description: We categorize based on a "family resemblance" rather than a strict definition of specific features. This is why it can be hard to define words, ideas.
fields.summary:
Cognitive scientific theory that suggests we categorize things and ideas according to a "family resemblance" rather than by requiring something have all necessary and sufficient conditions.

For example, you might think of a chair in your mind is defined by having four legs, a seat, and a backrest, but when you encounter an office chair or a stool with a backrest, the category divisions get fuzzy. Rather than throwing out the office chair, you accept it as a chair, even though it has a wheeled base instead of four legs. Maybe you decide the stool with the backrest is just a tall chair, or maybe it's a weird stool.

fields.title: AI 2027
fields.summary:
A scenario written by AI experts, Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, Thomas Larsen, Eli Lifland, and Romeo Dean, to help us forecast the potential future. The authors describe it as "our best guess about what that might look like. It’s informed by trend extrapolations, wargames, expert feedback, experience at OpenAI, and previous forecasting successes."

The usefulness of this document for the general public, I think, is in glimpsing the behind-the-scenes ideas and values of AI companies, their motivations and incentives, and especially in seeing what potential futures are ahead of us. Hopefully, we can use this to steer clear of the warning signs and towards a safe and healthy future with AI.
